title: hotpage-ejection-threshold-empirical-runbook
body:
Summary:

This note captures an exploratory runbook and empirical findings for a new heuristic we call 'hotpage ejection threshold' — an ejection policy tuned to reduce NVMe spill waves and memory-bandwidth driven latency spikes observed on mixed-seqlen workloads. The goal is to quantify how a tunable time/size threshold affects reuse rates, eviction churn, and observed device bandwidth when the KV cache is under pressure.

Context / Motivation:
- Recent production incidents (see ENG-2371) show short-lived eviction storms where pages cycle between GPU memory and NVMe repeatedly for a small hot working set, causing token-latency P95 regressions for tail workloads.
- Existing LRU-like policies evict by least-recently-used or lowest-priority score; they don't explicitly consider a cheap probation window that avoids ejecting pages which have a high short-term reuse probability.
- Hypothesis: Introducing a time-based ejection threshold (don't eject pages accessed within last T ms OR pages below X bytes of resident tensor size) reduces writeback waves and smooths bandwidth peaks, at modest memory residency cost.

Definitions used in experiments:
- hotpage: a page/frame holding KV entries with > 2 accesses in the last 2 seconds in baseline traces.
- ejection_threshold (T): time in milliseconds since last access below which page is protected from eviction.
- resident_bytes_cutoff (X): if page size < X, treat it as small-page-protected to avoid cold-but-tiny churn.
- spill_wave: a period where NVMe write throughput exceeds 60% of device saturation for > 250ms.

Experiment design:
- Workloads: 4 synthetic mixes created from production traces A,B,C,D (mixes: chat-short, chat-longtail, summarization, blended-multi-tenant). Traces sampled for realistic seqlen distributions and request concurrency.
- Hardware: A2 nodes (8x A100 equivalent) with NVMe backed local SSDs (measured baseline device BW ~ 6.8 GB/s), host memory 256GB.
- Runtime baseline: current release v1.18 with default LRU eviction + priority aging.
- Variants tested (each run 30 minutes steady-state, warmup 5 minutes):
  - baseline (no threshold)
  - T=50ms, X=0KB
  - T=250ms, X=0KB
  - T=1000ms, X=0KB
  - T=250ms, X=64KB
  - T=250ms, X=256KB
- Metrics collected: token latency P50/P95/P99, tokens/sec (throughput), NVMe write/read BW (per-second), eviction rate (pages/sec), refetch rate (pages/sec reloaded from NVMe), per-request extra latency attributed to spillback (sampling at request level).

Instrumentation notes:
- Used per-page access counters + last_access_ts exported through our runtime trace logs (devtool: page_event_log v0.3).
- Added a light-weight sampler to attach page eviction cause (explicit eviction vs prefetch reclaim) to the request trace for post-hoc attribution.
- Collected iostat-style NVMe counters and runtime internal BW counters, aligned by wall clock; small jitter corrected by linear interpolation.

Key empirical observations (high-level):
1) Bandwidth smoothing: T >= 250ms consistently reduced instantaneous NVMe write peaks. For chat-longtail, the 99th percentile per-second write BW decreased from 5.9 GB/s (baseline) to 3.6 GB/s (T=250ms).
2) Eviction churn: Eviction rate (pages/sec) dropped by ~28% at T=250ms, X=0KB. However, re-fetch rate (pages re-loaded within 5s of eviction) decreased by ~55%, indicating fewer oscillatory evictions.
3) Tail latency: Token P95 improved modestly on longtail mixes (median improvement 6–12%). On very short chat mixes, throughput decreased slightly with T=1000ms due to higher resident set occupancy and more frequent garbage compactions.
4) Small-page protection: Adding X=64KB reduced write amplification in blended workloads by preventing eviction of small frequently-accessed subcomponents, but X=256KB started to reserve too much memory and raised cold-miss rates for larger context pages.
5) Probation tradeoff: T too small (<100ms) provided little smoothing; T too large (>1000ms) protected pages that were effectively cold for certain tenant workloads and increased overall memory pressure leading to higher background compaction frequency.

Selected numeric excerpt (chat-longtail mix):
- Baseline: NVMe write P99 = 5.9 GB/s, eviction 180 pages/sec, re-fetch 75 pages/sec, token P95 = 164 ms
- T=250ms,X=0KB: NVMe write P99 = 3.6 GB/s, eviction 130 pages/sec, re-fetch 34 pages/sec, token P95 = 145 ms
- T=1000ms,X=0KB: NVMe write P99 = 3.3 GB/s, eviction 110 pages/sec, re-fetch 12 pages/sec, token P95 = 150 ms (throughput drop -3%)
- T=250ms,X=64KB: NVMe write P99 = 3.2 GB/s, eviction 125 pages/sec, re-fetch 28 pages/sec, token P95 = 142 ms

Qualitative traces and root-cause patterns:
- Observed sequences where a medium-size page (200KB) would toggle between GPU and NVMe every 1.2s causing a mini-wave: pattern of accesses separated by ~800–1200ms. T=250ms prevented the first eviction, which in baseline triggered a cascade because subsequent accesses happened shortly after eviction and forced immediate rehydration.
- Bandwidth spectrograms show correlated spikes with request bursts; smoothing reduces the amplitude and moves the work to steady-state background writeback which our NVMe queue handles better.

Risks and failure modes:
- Memory oversubscription: protecting pages increases resident set size; under memory-constrained nodes this can cause OOM or more aggressive compaction. Must combine threshold with admission controls or increase low-priority eviction pressure for pages that exceed both time and size limits.
- Multi-tenant fairness: a tenant with high short-term reuse could monopolize protected slots. Need per-tenant protection quotas.
- Workload drift: the ideal T depends on temporal locality of workload; adaptive T may be needed.

Short proposal for a minimal safe rollout (canary path):
1) Implement ejection_threshold as a soft-protection flag evaluated in the evictor. Rule: skip eviction if (now - last_access) < T AND page_size <= S_max OR page_access_count >= 2 in last window.
2) Expose T and X as node-level config with defaults: T=250ms, X=128KB. Default conservative until telemetry proves stable.
3) Add telemetry dashboards: live eviction rate, re-fetch rate, NVMe per-second P50/P95, protected-resident-bytes (how much memory currently protected by threshold).
4) Canary rollout: 5% of serving runtime fleet under blended-mix; monitor gamma metrics for 24h before expanding.

Open questions / follow-ups:
- Adaptive threshold: can we compute T per-page using a short-term exponential moving average of inter-access times? Early sketch shows promise but requires more complex book-keeping.
- Per-tenant quotas: design and safety checks to avoid one tenant consuming all protected slots.
- Interaction with prefetcher: when we protect pages we may reduce prefetch effectiveness for other pages; need to test with prefetch on/off.
- Long-running stability: 7-day soak run to observe compaction/backpressure behavior on real traffic.

Immediate action items:
- [Evan] Create GH PR to add ejection_threshold config and lightweight last_access check (draft branch: evict-threshold-sketch). Link: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/412
- [Maya] Build telemetry panels for protected-resident-bytes and re-fetch attribution.
- [Luis] Run 24h canary on blend-05 nodepool with T=250ms,X=64KB; collect traces and upload raw logs to s3://redwood-experiments/hotpage-ejection/2025-11-05
- [Team] Prepare automated test that asserts shared fairness (no tenant > 30% of protected-resident-bytes)

Notes to self:
- This heuristic is intentionally conservative — protect short-lived hotpages long enough to absorb short bursts but small enough to avoid long-term leakage.
- When writing the PR keep code-paths separate and well-instrumented; we want to revert quickly if regression.

Appendix: quick checklist for reproducing locally:
1) Checkout branch evict-threshold-sketch and build dev image.
2) Use trace-synth tool with sample file traces/chat-longtail-2025-08.sample.json
3) Start runtime with config: {"evict_policy":"lru","eject_threshold_ms":250,"eject_resident_cutoff_kb":64} (dev CLI flag: --eject-threshold-ms, --eject-resident-cutoff-kb)
4) Run loadgen 3000 qps for 30m, collect /metrics and /internal/page_event_log
5) Post-process with analyze_evictions.py (script in tools/eviction-audit)

If you want, I can convert this runbook into a short RFC for product to weigh in on defaults + SLA implications.

-- Evan
